slides.notes:
User configuration: analog BS and UE; BS beam grid 10 by 10; UE beam grid 8 by 4; one pilot symbol. Physical antenna dimensions are retained, not inferred from beam counts.

elements.html: Analog beam sweeping at the BS and UE · revised 29 September 2026

100 BS beams. 32 UE beams.
One pilot symbol per beam pair.
Known beam weights and pilots. Unknown delay, AoA, AoD, path gain and receiver clock. Retain the complex I/Q after analog combining.
One symbol means one OFDM symbol at each tested pair—not one symbol for the full sweep.

slides.notes:
The CRB is a matrix lower bound, not a guarantee of an attainable estimator. Detection probability and the unknown number of paths are different statistical problems. A singular direction has no ordinary finite local CRB. Results in this deck are conditional on one path except the explicitly identified multipath gain illustration.

elements.html: Beam counts are not antenna counts
Keep hardware, codebook size and training duration separate.

BS beam grid: 10 × 10 = 100 beams.

UE beam grid: 8 × 4 = 32 beams.

Pilot: one OFDM symbol per pair.

One complex receiver output per tone after analog combining.

BS array: 24 × 16 = 384 elements.
UE array: 8 × 4 = 32 elements.

27.2 GHz carrier; λ/2 spacing.
3300 pilot tones over 400 MHz.

Array sizes are inherited from the earlier deck. Beam grid sizes do not specify physical antenna counts.

slides.notes:
The mean is a specialization of the path-based OFDM model to a single analog transmit vector and receive vector per acquisition. Conventional phase-shifter weights are frequency-independent within each symbol. The array model here uses narrowband steering at the carrier; beam squint is excluded and requires frequency-dependent array responses. All complex I/Q values are retained, not only beam powers.

ONE SCALAR PER PAIR AND TONE

\[y_{mnk}=s_k\mathbf w_n^H\widetilde{\mathbf H}_k\mathbf v_m+z_{mnk}\]\[\widetilde{\mathbf H}_k=e^{-j2\pi f_kb}\mathbf H_k^{\rm g}\]m = 1, …, 100 BS beams.
n = 1, …, 32 UE combiners.
k indexes pilot tones.

The one-symbol index is suppressed.

\[\mu_{mnk}=s_k\alpha e^{-j2\pi f_k\tau^{\rm a}}r_n t_m\]\[r_n=\mathbf w_n^H\mathbf a_r,\quad t_m=\mathbf a_t^H\mathbf v_m\]\[\tau^{\rm a}=\tau^{\rm g}+b\]Angles enter the known beam responses. The channel and complex gain remain unknown.

slides.notes:
Derived counts assume one useful OFDM symbol at every pair, 3300 contiguous active bins and B=K delta f=400 MHz. Useful time is 26.4 ms; it is not an assertion about hardware latency or channel coherence. The 10 by 10 and 8 by 4 dimensions describe azimuth/elevation codebook grids under the interpretation used here.

elements.html: One symbol per pair is 3,200 symbols per sweep
This count assumes every BS beam is tested against every UE beam.
\[M=10\times10=100,\quad N=8\times4=32\]\[Q=MN=3200\]\[N_{\rm samples}=QK=10{,}560{,}000\]Each sample is a complex scalar. Sequential beam settings are not simultaneous RF outputs.

\[\Delta f=B/K=121.212\ {\rm kHz}\]\[T_u=1/\Delta f=8.25\ \mu{\rm s}\]\[T_{\rm sweep}=Q/\Delta f=26.4\ {\rm ms}\]Add CP, beam switching and scheduling gaps. A reduced schedule uses its actual pair count.

slides.notes:
The noise is proper circular complex Gaussian with known parameter-independent variance. Stack derivatives over the scheduled scalar observations; J=2 Re(D^H C^-1 D). The browser accumulates exact tone moments and spatial derivatives, algebraically equivalent to summing every raw sample. Parameter units are ns, degrees, degrees, degrees, degrees, dB, radians. Full joint marginal bounds include gain/phase nuisance coupling.

elements.html: Differentiate the swept mean, not the old pilots
The actual beam responses and acquisition schedule determine the Fisher matrix.

\[J_{ij}=2\operatorname{Re}\sum_{(m,n)\in\mathcal S}\sum_k\frac{(\partial_i\mu_{mnk})^*(\partial_j\mu_{mnk})}{\sigma_{mnk}^2}\]\[\boldsymbol\eta=[\tau^{\rm a},\varphi_r,\epsilon_r,\varphi_t,\epsilon_t,\ell,\phi]^T\]Unknown attenuation and phase are included, not held fixed.

\[\partial_{q_r}\mu=s_k\alpha e^{-j2\pi f_k\tau^{\rm a}}(\partial_{q_r}r_n)t_m\]\[\partial_{q_t}\mu=s_k\alpha e^{-j2\pi f_k\tau^{\rm a}}r_n(\partial_{q_t}t_m)\]\[\partial_{\tau^{\rm a}}\mu=-j2\pi f_k\mu\]Invert the identifiable joint information—not only its diagonal entries.

slides.notes:
A single fixed beam pair generally cannot identify AoA/AoD jointly with a free complex gain in the stated frequency-flat array-response model. Across a coherent sweep the gain is shared but the known responses vary; full rank is possible, not guaranteed. Beam coverage, calibration, physical aperture and chosen operating point matter. Beam squint can alter the single-pair conclusion and is not modeled here.

elements.html: A short pilot can still provide spatial diversity
One symbol at many pairs is different from repeating one fixed pair.

\[\alpha_{\rm eff}=\alpha\,r_n(\mathbf q_r)\,t_m(\mathbf q_t)\]Under narrowband steering, all four angles enter one unknown complex scalar.

A free gain can absorb their effect.

Frequency diversity can retain delay information, but does not supply the missing spatial diversity.

Different known beam responses reveal angle-dependent changes across the schedule.

\[\operatorname{rank}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{Re}\mathbf D\\\operatorname{Im}\mathbf D\end{bmatrix}\]determines local identifiability.

No requirement of 384 symbols per pair. Check the structured Jacobian, not the old time-code rank condition.

slides.notes:
Useful sweep duration is not a coherence guarantee. For a moving channel, angles, delay and gain can vary as well as Doppler phase. One symbol per pair does not remove the time spread of the whole schedule. Unknown pairwise phases change the nuisance structure; independent arbitrary complex pair gains can remove spatial identifiability. The CRB shown is conditional on the static coherent likelihood.

elements.html: A 26.4 ms useful sweep must not silently become one simultaneous snapshot.

One static isolated far-field path.

A common complex gain and stable or compensated phase across beam pairs.

Known, calibrated beam weights.

Retained complex I/Q, not just received power or the index of the strongest beam.

\[\mu_{mnk}\ \mapsto\ \mu_{mnk}e^{j2\pi\nu t_{mn}}\]Retain timestamps and Doppler for motion.

Model switching offsets, phase noise and calibration uncertainty as appropriate nuisance parameters.

Power-only data need a different likelihood.

slides.notes:
Unit-modulus array steering and unit-norm RF weights keep transmit power and receive noise consistent. Pre-combining noise is spatially white with independent realizations at sequential pairs. An aligned beam can gain Nt or Nr in signal power, already captured in the responses; never multiply those gains in again. Noise figure includes whatever effective RF loss is assumed. Default ideal beams form uniform azimuth/elevation grids covering -60 to 60 and -30 to 30 degrees at both ends. These coverage choices, power=30 dBm and loss=120 dB are teaching inputs, not user-supplied measured hardware settings.

elements.html: Known training does not mean a known channel
The receiver knows the experiment. It must estimate the propagation parameters.

Pilot values and subcarrier frequencies.

BS beam weights and UE combiner weights.

Beam-pair schedule and timestamps.

Array calibration and the assumed noise covariance.

Each path’s apparent delay, two arrival angles, two departure angles, attenuation and phase.

The receiver clock and the number of paths are unknown.

The true channel is used only to evaluate the CRB—not as an estimator input.

slides.notes:
With free geometric delays and common clock, the Fisher matrix has the gauge direction (-delta,...,-delta,+delta). Common carrier phase is absorbed into the free path gains. Multiplication by analog weights does not change this invariance. The geometry section remains applicable after using the correct beam-sweep channel information.

elements.html: Beam sweeping does not resolve the clock gauge
Every path still contains the same receiver timing bias.

\[\mu_{mnk}=s_k\sum_p\alpha_p e^{-j2\pi f_k(\tau_p^{\rm g}+b)}r_{np}t_{mp}\]\[\partial_b\mu_{mnk}=\sum_p\partial_{\tau_p^{\rm g}}\mu_{mnk}\]Adding δ to b and subtracting δ from every geometric delay leaves all samples unchanged.

\[\tau_p^{\rm a}=\tau_p^{\rm g}+b\]Channel-level CRBs refer to apparent delay.

Delay differences cancel the common clock.

A clock reference, prior or geometric constraints are additional information, not a benefit of extra beam pairs alone.

slides.notes:
In 3D the UE has 3 position, 3 orientation and 1 clock unknowns. The LoS path gives 5 measurements. With one single-bounce path: the two AoDs fix the rays from the BS to the UE and to v; the LoS AoA fixes UE orientation up to roll about the LoS axis; the bounce AoA fixes that roll and the ratio of the two ray lengths; the delay difference sets the scale. Then b equals tau_1^a minus range over c. Counting is necessary, not sufficient: degenerate placements, such as v on the BS-UE line, lose rank. The bound on b comes from inverting the geometric FIM after mapping every path to the common unknowns, as on the radio SLAM slide.

elements.html: Geometry, not the channel, separates the clock
Every apparent delay shares one b. The paths tie it to the unknown UE pose and map.

\[c\,\tau^{\mathrm a}_1=\|\mathbf x-\mathbf p_{\mathrm{BS}}\|+c\,b\]UE unknowns: 3 position, 3 orientation, 1 clock. LoS supplies 5 measurements.

AoD fixes the ray from the known BS. Along that ray, a longer range and an earlier clock give the same \(\tau^{\mathrm a}_1\).

b is not identifiable.

\[c\,\tau^{\mathrm a}_2=\|\mathbf v-\mathbf p_{\mathrm{BS}}\|+\|\mathbf x-\mathbf v\|+c\,b\]The incidence point v is unknown: 5 new measurements, 3 new unknowns. Now 10 and 10.

The bounce AoA fixes the UE roll and the ratio of ray lengths. The delay difference sets the scale.

For generic geometry \(\mathbf H^T\mathbf J_\eta\mathbf H\) becomes full rank and b has a finite bound.

THREE WAYS TO SET THE DEMO

Aggregate SNR: hold Γ fixed to isolate frequency spread or aperture.

Per-tone SNR: hold ρ fixed. More tones, receivers, or symbols add information.

Power and noise: calculate ρ from the physical link budget.
